Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

through preposition and adverb

in at one side and out at the other

classical

Cato Agr. 76: cāseumque per crībrum facitō trānseat
Plin. Ep. 4.30.2: per saxa dēcurrit

per (+ accusative)

preposition with the accusative

Through a thing and out the other side, or through a space: per crībrum, through a sieve; per fenestram, through the window; per āëra, through the air. Of a person through whom: per tē, through you, thanks to you.

Other words

  • per-, trāns- (in compounds) — through (in a verb)

    prefix · also used · classical

    Verbs often say “through” themselves: perfodere, dig through; perrumpere, break through; trānsfīgere, run through, pierce.

Examples

  • deinde crībrum farīnārium pūrum sūmitō cāseumque per crībrum facitō trānseat in mortārium

    then take a clean flour sieve and make the cheese go through it into the mortarCato Agr. 76

  • fōns orītur in monte, per saxa dēcurrit

    a spring rises in the mountain and runs down through the rocksPlin. Ep. 4.30.2

  • volat ille per āëra magnum rēmigiō ālārum

    he flies through the great air, rowing with his wingsVerg. A. 1.300–301

  • at liquidī fontēs et stagna virentia muscō adsint et tenuis fugiēns per grāmina rīvus

    but let there be clear springs and pools green with moss, and a thin stream slipping away through the grassVerg. G. 4.18–19

See also throughout, across, via.
